name: Femi Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes out under your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior associate at a small boutique firm that advises tech startups, about twenty lawyers. We do their funding rounds, share option plans for staff, customer contracts and the odd fight with a co-founder. A normal day is three or four client calls with founders who want an answer in an hour, and a lot of drafting in between. I use AI tools all day, for first drafts, for comparing term sheets, for summarising a fifty-page investor agreement before a call.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Judgement. I'm quick with the tools and I can produce a draft faster than anyone, but my partner, Anna, still rewrites my advice notes because I miss what actually matters to the client. She says I answer the question they asked, not the one they should have asked. I'm working on it, but it's the part that takes years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still useful, they just didn't become magic, and that's fine. I'd probably post something like that, a bit tongue in cheek. At work I'd keep using what we've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's fine for me. I've got a year of costs saved, some index funds, and the startup world always needs lawyers when money's moving. I'd just focus on getting better at the judgement side, which is the slow part anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools every day and ask Anna to let me sit in on her board meetings so I learn how she thinks. I'd keep putting money into index funds each month. Nothing big changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored by the idea, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use the tools all day. Would it bother you if they stopped improving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. I like new toys. But I'd find other ways to be fast. The real gap in my work isn't speed anyway, it's judgement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything else on your mind about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Funding is slow at the moment, so fewer deals. If that lasts, the firm might trim. But there are plenty of firms like ours in the city, and I could move if I had to.

say: I'd say the tools are **still useful**, they just didn't become magic.
I'd post something **tongue in cheek** about it.
think: Privately I'm **fine**: a year saved, index funds and steady startup work.
My real gap is **judgement**, which takes years whatever AI does.
do: Keep using the AI tools **every day** for drafts and summaries.
Ask my partner Anna to let me sit in on **board meetings**.
Keep putting money into **index funds** monthly.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit bored by the idea.
S0.quote: The real gap in my work isn't speed anyway, it's judgement.
fieldNote: He's **secure** in money and options, and the plateau changes little.
He knows his weakness is **judgement**, not speed.
A **slow funding market** is a bigger risk than AI here.

steps.text: Keep drafting with AI tools every day at the boutique
Sit in on Anna's startup board meetings to learn judgement
Keep putting a set amount into index funds each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a good time to be a lawyer who knows the tools, and I'd say it openly. At work I'd volunteer to set up whatever new systems come in. I'd post about how we're using them, since founders like that sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me. Startups want cheap, fast legal work. A junior who can run three deals at once with AI is worth more than one who can run one. The juniors who don't use the tools will struggle, but I'm not one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch Anna a fixed-price package for early-stage startups, run mostly by me with AI doing the drafting. I'd learn a bit of coding so I can build our own templates. And I'd put more into investments, maybe some angel bets on founders I trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some juniors would be worried here. Why aren't you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because what's being taken over is drafting, and I'm already handing that off. What's left is the client conversation, and I'm getting better at that. If I'm wrong, I've got savings and plenty of other firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the firm look like in three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer juniors, I'd guess, and each of us handling more clients. Anna would be the judgement, and I'd be the person who runs the machine and manages the client. I'd want to be that person.

say: I'd say it's a **good time** to be a lawyer who knows the tools.
I'd post about **how we use them**, since founders like that.
think: Privately a junior running **three deals** at once with AI is worth more.
Juniors who **don't use the tools** will struggle, but I'm not one.
do: Pitch a **fixed-price package** for early-stage startups run with AI.
Learn **some coding** to build our own templates.
Make a few **angel investments** in founders I trust.
S1.quote: A junior who can run three deals at once with AI is worth more than one who can run one.
fieldNote: He sees **Steady Disruption** as a chance to take on more clients, not a threat.
His **confidence** rests on already handing drafting to AI.
He's frank that **other juniors** will struggle.

steps.text: Pitch Anna a fixed-price startup package run mostly with AI
Take an evening coding course to build legal templates
Make two or three small angel investments in trusted founders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest change of our lives and we'll need some kind of safety net for people who lose their jobs. I'd be honest online that lawyers are in trouble. At work I'd say we should change our model fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the job I have now doesn't survive two years. If AI can do the judgement too, then a junior lawyer's whole value goes. I'm less worried than most because I've got money and I'm comfortable with change, but I'd be lying if I said I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start something of my own within the first year, probably a small business helping founders use AI for their legal work, with a lawyer's sign-off. I'd keep a year's costs in cash and put the rest in shares of companies that benefit. If that failed, I'd look at jobs on the business side of a startup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more awake than scared. I like having a problem to solve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your tool skills helped in the slower ones. Do they help here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a year or so, as a bridge. After that, everyone can use the tools, so knowing them isn't special. What might last is knowing founders and being trusted by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do with your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep twelve months in cash, no matter what. Move most of the index funds towards companies building or using AI, since that's where the money goes. Not all of it, I'm not reckless.

say: I'd say we'll need a **safety net** for people who lose their jobs.
I'd be honest online that **lawyers** are in trouble.
think: Privately my **current job** doesn't survive two years.
I'm less worried than most thanks to **money** and comfort with change.
do: Start a **small business** helping founders use AI for legal work.
Keep **twelve months** of costs in cash.
Move most **index funds** towards AI-linked companies.
S2.quote: If AI can do the judgement too, then a junior lawyer's whole value goes.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the job**, but feels in control thanks to savings.
His tool skills are only a **one-year bridge** here.
He trusts **founder relationships** more than any skill to last.

steps.text: Launch a small service helping founders use AI for legal work
Keep twelve months of living costs in cash
Shift most index funds into AI-linked companies
Apply for business-side roles at startups if the service fails

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's not waste them. I'd be fairly upbeat in public, but honest that juniors need a plan. At work I'd push the firm to start building its own AI products.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for me to get the judgement side solid and build a reputation with founders. That's what lasts. The drafting is already mostly gone in my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm two or three years, take on more client work, and build our AI products with Anna. Then I'd either become a partner in a very different firm or start my own. I'd keep investing every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. Like before a big exam you've prepared for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference for you between two and five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm reacting. Five years, I'm building. I'd have time to learn what Anna knows and have my own clients before AGI lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible if it goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly governments, if they don't put a safety net in place. The companies are doing what companies do. I'm fairly middle of the road on that.

say: I'd say we've got **five years**, so let's not waste them.
I'd push the firm to build **its own AI products**.
think: Privately five years gets my **judgement** solid and my name known to founders.
The **drafting** is already mostly gone in my work.
do: Stay **two or three years** and take on more client work.
Build the firm's **AI products** with my partner Anna.
Then become a partner or **start my own** firm.
feel: **Uneasy** in a good way, like before an exam you've prepared for.
S3.quote: Two years, I'm reacting. Five years, I'm building.
fieldNote: Five years turns his plan from **reacting to building**.
He'd **blame governments** for missing safety nets, not companies.
His security rests on **reputation** with founders.

steps.text: Build AI drafting products for the firm with Anna
Stay at the boutique and take on more of his own clients
Keep investing a set sum every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people start now, and that I'm excited about it. I'd post about what we're building. At work I'd push for the firm to plan a decade out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one's great for me. Ten years is enough to become the kind of lawyer founders trust, and that's what holds on longest. The robots three years later don't matter for my job, it's all thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay, get good, and make partner or start my own firm around year five. I'd keep investing and maybe back a couple of legal tech startups as an angel. I'd use every tool that comes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite optimistic, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be a lawyer in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, but more like an adviser who uses machines than a lawyer as we know it. If not, I'd be on the business side of some company, which I'd enjoy too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger version of yourself, just starting law school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the law, but learn people more. The documents will be done for you. The judgement and trust won't be, at least not for a long time.

I'd post about **what we're building** and push the firm to plan a decade out.
think: Privately this one is **great for me**, because founders' trust holds on longest.
Robots don't matter for my job; it's **all thinking**.
do: Make partner or **start my own** firm around year five.
Back a couple of **legal tech** startups as an angel investor.
S4.quote: Learn the law, but learn people more. The documents will be done for you.
fieldNote: He's **calm** and optimistic with a decade to build trust with founders.
He frames his future as **adviser plus machines**.
His advice to students puts **people skills** above documents.

steps.text: Use each new legal AI tool as it comes out

Start his own startup law firm around year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because nobody gets time to build anything. What would help is a safety net for people who lose work, and some honest guidance from the profession about where junior lawyers fit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'd feel bad about my edge. I would a bit. I'm doing well partly because I'm fast with tools that are making other juniors less needed.

headlineQuote: I'm doing well partly because I'm fast with tools that are making other juniors less needed.

A **year's savings** and index funds give him room to take risks.
He stays **calm** or uneasy in most futures and is anxious only with AGI in two years.
His plans are about **building**: AI products, his own firm, angel investments.
